purpose:
Chichester Business Improvement District (BID)
is nearing the end of its five-year term and wishes to seek renewal
for a further term of five years. This report will set out the
background to the BID, the renewal process and the financial
implications, and seeks approval from Members for the ballot
process to be undertaken. Cabinet will be requested that the
Council be recommended to delegate to the Leader the authority to
vote in accordance with Cabinet’s decision in relation to the
ballot to renew the BID.
content:
Resolved:
 
1.2 Cabinet notes
the ‘Renewal Business Proposal’ prepared by Chichester
Business Improvement District (BID) and supports the renewal of the
BID for a further term of five years.
 
1.3 Subject to 1.2
Cabinet recommends to Council to approve authority for the Leader
to represent the council to vote to support the BID in the BID
ballot.
 
1.4 Cabinet approves
that the ballot holder, the Divisional Manager for Business
Support, as the council’s Returning Officer, be instructed to
hold the BID ballot.
 
1.5 Subject to 1.2
Cabinet approves the additional budget requirement, of
£10,000 to cover Chichester District Council’s
increased BID levy payment, from 2027/28 onwards.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to support the renewal of the Chichester Business Improvement District (BID) for another five years.

purpose:
To approve the draft Southbourne Development
Plan Document for a period of consultation of 6 weeks, prior to
submission for examination.
content:
Resolved:
 
2.1 That Cabinet
recommends to Council that:
 
1. The Southbourne
Allocation Development Plan Document 2021 – 2039 (Submission
Version) be approved for a 6-week public consultation from 5 June
2026 to 17 July 2026 under Regulation 19 of the Town and Country
Planning (England) Regulations 2012 (as amended);
 
2. Following
publication and consultation, the Southbourne Allocation
Development Plan Document 2021 – 2039 (Submission Version)
and supporting documents be submitted to the Secretary of State for
examination, together with the representations made under
Regulation 20 (in response to consultation at Regulation 19) and a
summary thereof (as an update to the Statement of
Consultation);
 
3. The Director of
Planning and the Environment be authorised, following consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Planning Services, to:
 

a.   
 make minor amendments and any
necessary editorial changes to the submission version of the
Southbourne Allocation DPD 2021 – 2039, (Regulation 19), the
Submission Policies Map, the Sustainability Appraisal and Habitats
Regulations Assessment, prior to publication, prior to submission
and during the examination;

 

b.   
prepare the Council’s response to the main issues
identified and to any substantial concerns about soundness or legal
compliance raised in the representations, to submit alongside the
DPD;

 

c.   
if necessary, prepare a Schedule of Main Modifications that may
be necessary to address soundness issues raised by representations
received in response to the Regulation 19 publication, that can be
submitted with the DPD to be considered by the Inspector during the
examination process; and

 

d.   
if necessary, prepare a Schedule of Minor Modifications that may
be necessary to address minor editorial and factual changes that do
not go to the soundness of the plan that can be submitted with the
DPD to be considered by the Inspector during the examination
process.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Southbourne Allocation Development Plan Document 2021-2039 for public consultation and submission to the Secretary of State for examination.

content:
The following public question
and answers were received:
 
Question from Mr Philip Maber
 
"My question topic
is when can the CDC Contaminated Sites Register include the
Star Energy (was IGas) Oil Extraction Site hidden within Singleton
Forest (my near neighbour), please?
 
Our Singleton Forest Watch
campaign Group has accumulated significant knowledge on the 30+
years of high pressure pumped injection (dumping) of waste liquids
into the Ashdown Sandstone Beds Aquifer. Up to a 50 m Olympic
Swimming pool equivalent per a month is now permitted by
Environment Agency Permit (2021). Prior to 2016 this below ground
activity was unregulated.
 
The Environment Agency has
designated the Ashdown Sandstone Aquifer as unsuitable for
future use.
 
Highly Toxic waste was also
being brought in from other sites, at least up to 2021, when the
SDNPA managed a verbal agreement with IGas to restrict the
injection to only waste liquid produced on site.
 
This SDNPA restriction is
because Minerals Planning Permission is also required (and never
been issued).
 
However, in c.2023 The
Environment Agency Granted a Permit for the importation and storage
of radioactive waste at Singleton.
 
SDNPA has confirmed that no
Planning Application has been submitted, and that any such
Application would include the requirement for an Environmental
Impact Assessment (IEA). No such IEA to date.
 
Truth is
that nobody knows what is going on in Singleton Forest
(commercial confidentiality), and that many polluting activities
remain unregulated - EA Permits issued without limits.
 
The cumulative spread of the
waste liquid has logically extended for many miles. Officially
referred to as Produced
Water and Naturally Occurring Radioactive
Material (NORM) - it is saline, with heavy metals, and a
cocktail of chemicals used to stimulate the oil from the Oolite
rock strata, plus chemicals and biocides used to clean and protect
the well linings. I understand each well has to be cleaned every
two months (that's a mile+ down, together with unknown miles of
horizontal extraction well). Each well requires a full well
Makeover every 2 to 3 years - involving the use of a rig tower and
other specialist equipment.
 
The actual crude oil produced
is a small proportion of the total liquids and gasses
produced.
 
Documented contamination of our
vital chalk aquifer occured in the 1990s via 'cracked well
casings'. Most of the monitoring water boreholes now appear long
derelict.
 
We now understand that 12 wells
have been drilled at Singleton, with 6 in current production and
the one shallower, waste injection well.
 
Each of these wells provides an
annulus route for the highly pressurised, injected waste liquid to
travel upwards though the clay into the chalk
aquifer.
 
Please consider too, the
lubrication provided by the injected waste in an area of known
geological fault and seismic activity.
 
Singleton Forest and an unknown
area around, is very contaminated site, and must be
recognised as such, please?
The increasing threat of
horrendous environmental consequence must be on
public register.
 
Answer from Cllr
Jonathan Brown
 
Thank you for your question, Mr Maber.
 
I note that you have previously asked similar
questions by e-mails to officers. You were provided with a full
reply by email on the 9th April 2026, and I refer you
back to that reply as it explains the council’s position in
full.
 
To summarise, the council’s duties with
regard to land contamination are defined in statute with supporting
statutory guidance. Paragraph 4.40 (C) of the statutory guidance is
clear that sites cannot be considered to be Contaminated Land on
water pollution grounds where the substances entered the water in
compliance with a discharge authorised under the Environmental
Permitting Regulations. We understand this to be the case here and
so the permitted process and the land affected by its activities
cannot be determined as Contaminated Land. The site cannot
therefore appear on the council’s register of Contaminated
Land sites.
 
As you are aware the site is subject to a
Pollution Control Permit for its oil drilling and ancillary
activities which was issued and is enforced by the Environment
Agency (EA) as the regulator. Officers of the council have
previously advised you that questions relating to the control of
activities on the site should be directed to the EA and that
remains the case.
Likewise, questions about the mineral planning
aspects of the site should be directed at the South Downs National
Park Authority as the Mineral Planning Authority.
 
Supplement from Mr
Maber
 
Given that the
Environment Agency funding has been severely reduced, could CDC
initiate a site assessment, please?
A Hydrogeological
Survey is a must - How far has the contamination spread? Where
has, and will, it further impact our environment and water
resources? Recorded and confirmed hydrocarbon contamination of our
Chalk Aquifer.
 
Air
Quality: 
 

a.              
 Will the plumes of putrid black smoke be curtailed when
the hitherto waste gas is partly utilised in the, yet to be
commissioned, mini-power-station?
 

b.             
Will the vented and fugetively emitted plumes of methane
and other volatile organic compounds stop … 80 x the Green
House Heating of CO2 in a 20-year period.
 

c.              
How radioactive is the site - black soot on a cherry tree
outside the perimeter fence is long suspected as a severe health
concern.
 
I suggest the
Environment Agency's inabilities are a big driver of CDC support
for the Western Sussex Rivers Trust - mega thank you!
 
Answer to the
supplementary question from Mr Maber:
 
Thank you for your supplementary question. The
council will not instigate a site assessment at the site. The
statutory guidance is clear that the council should seek advice
from the EA on matters relating to groundwater and in any case, as
explained in our written answer and in answer to part one of your
question today, the statutory guidance is also clear that the site
cannot be determined as Contaminated Land where the alleged
pollution has entered the ground water under the auspices of a
permit. The EA are aware of the council’s position in this
regard.
 
Issues regarding smoke and other gases emitted
from the site are matters for the EA to consider under the auspices
of the Permit issued to the site.
 
Cllr Brown further expressed his support for
chasing up agencies and offered to liaise further with Mr Maber
outside the meeting.
topline: The CDC has decided not to include the Star Energy Oil Extraction Site in Singleton Forest on the Contaminated Sites Register, despite concerns raised by local stakeholders about contamination and pollution.

enforcement of housing standards in the private sector. This Policy
is revised in light of the Renters Rights Act 2025, and separated
out from the Housing Financial Assistance Policy where it
previously sat.
content:

minor amendments to the policy.

purpose:
To consider the Treasury Management Policy
Statement, the Treasury Management Strategy Statement, the
Investment Strategy and relevant indicators for 2026-27
content:
RESOLVED
 
That the Cabinet
approves the additional paragraphs to be added to the Treasury
Management Policy Statement, which was approved by the Corporate
Governance and Audit Committee at its meeting 19 January 2026.
 
“The Council
should report their treasury management indicators as detailed in
the sector specific guidance notes; these are set out in an
appendix to the Treasury Management Strategy Statement for the
Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Indicators of this
report for the forthcoming year and will be reported for the
outturn in the July after the year end.
 
Although The
Prudential Code requires the Prudential Indicators are reported
quarterly, the Council considers that its Outturn report and the
Half Yearly report provide sufficient information as required by
the Code and present the Council’s current debt free
position.”
 
RECOMMENDATION TO
COUNCIL
 
That the Cabinet
considers the Council’s draft Treasury Management and
Investment Strategy 2026-27 and recommends it to the Council for
approval.

purpose:
To set a net budget requirement and the
Council Tax for the Council for the financial year
2026-27
content:
RECOMMENDATION TO
COUNCIL
 
That the Cabinet
recommends to Council:
 
(a) That a net
budget requirement of £18,133,500 for 2026-27 be
approved;
 
(b) That Council Tax
be increased by £5.74 from £192.06 to £197.80 for
a Band D equivalent in 2026-27;
 
(c) That the
forecast budget surplus of £145,100 be transferred to the
General Fund Reserve;
 
(d) The capital
programme, including the asset renewal programme (appendices 1c and
1d of the agenda report) be approved;
 
(e) The capital
prudential indicators and the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP)
Policy (appendix 3 of the agenda report) be approved;
 
RESOLVED
 
That the Cabinet
notes:
 
a) The growth items
that have been incorporated into the base budget from 2026-27 as
detailed in paragraph 2.16 of the report;
 
b) The growth items
that have been incorporated into the base budget as one off
commitments for 2026-27 as detailed in paragraphs 2.17 and 2.18 of
the report;
 
That the Cabinet
further notes:
 
(a) The current
estimated reserves position set out in appendix 2 of the agenda
report, and
 
(b) The budget
variances included in the Draft Budget Spending Plan as set out in
appendix 1b of the agenda report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a net budget requirement for 2026-27, increase Council Tax, transfer a forecast budget surplus to the General Fund Reserve, approve the capital programme, and approve capital prudential indicators and the Minimum Revenue Provision Policy.
